t: The Garamantes mined fossil water from under the desert through a network of tunnels and shafts, the foggaras, which supported farming and a large population in the Fezzan.
Their largest town, Garama, had about four thousand inhabitants, with another six thousand in villages within a 5 km radius, and up to 50,000 people may have lived in the whole wadi.
The fall of the ground water level over the centuries of the kingdom may have contributed to its end in the late 7th century CE.
dyk: The Roman traveller Julius Maternus journeyed with the king of the Garamantes for about four months from Garama to a land called Agisymba, whose people the king presented as his subjects.
ev: Peoples who may have descended from Berber and Toubou tribes and Saharan pastoralists are settled in the Fezzan
The Garamantes form a powerful polity controlling trade routes between the Niger Bend and the Mediterranean
Herodotus describes the Garamantes as a very great nation who herded cattle and farmed dates
Lucius Cornelius Balbus and other Romans capture fifteen Garamantian settlements in response to continuous raiding
Septimius Severus captures the capital city of Garama
The Garamantian kingdom comes to an end as the ground water level falls

f.homeland: The Fezzan region of southern Libya, centred on the Wadi al-Ajjal; their capital Garama lay at modern Germa, about 150 km west of Sabha, with an earlier capital at Zinkekara; other sites include Fewet, Saniat bin Huwaydi, and the southern oases of Ghat and Barkat
f.period: Settlement in the Fezzan at least as early as 1000 BCE; a powerful polity from the 6th century BCE; foggara irrigation appearing between 200 BCE and 200 CE; a major regional power from the mid-2nd century CE; the end of the kingdom in the late 7th century CE
f.known: foggara (qanat) irrigation tapping fossil water; the first urban society in a major desert not centred on a river; control of trade routes between the Niger Bend, Lake Chad and the Mediterranean; slave raiding and trading; inscriptions in a Libyan script that are only partly decipherable; conflict with Rome
f.sources: Greco-Roman writers from Herodotus in the 5th century BCE to Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny the Elder, Ptolemy and Solinus; excavations at Germa in the 1960s; satellite imagery published in 2011; skeletal and isotopic studies by Sergi (1951), Chamla (1968), Mattingly et al. (2003), Lahr et al. (2010), Nikita et al. (2011), Ricci et al. (2013) and Power et al. (2019)
